spotlights.text: Dataset Spotlight: Common Voice ArabicCommon Voice is a crowd-sourced, openly licensed corpus in which volunteers read sentences aloud and others validate the recordings [13].Its Arabic portion is read rather than spontaneous speech, and its coverage of dialects is uneven, so it is not a complete picture of the language. But its permissive license and easy access make it the ideal starting point for the labs in this book: every reader can download it and run experiments without special agreements, provided each lab states the release version, the validated split, and the license alongside its results.

Dataset Spotlight: the KACST Arabic Phonetics Database (KAPD) [6], [28]Descriptive resources for Arabic phonetics and phonology [6], together with the King Abdulaziz City for Science and Technology (KACST) Arabic Phonetics Database (KAPD), a corpus of more than 46,000 files of articulatory and acoustic measurements from nine experiments with native speakers [28], provide carefully documented sound inventories and example words.Such resources can be converted into a pronunciation lexicon, the table that maps each word to its sequence of phones, which both classical recognizers (Chapter 4) and synthesizers (Chapter 9) depend on. The companion notebook for this chapter builds a small lexicon of this kind.

Dataset Spotlight: Common Voice Arabic for front-end experimentsThe crowd-sourced and validated Common Voice Arabic corpus [17] gives short read-speech clips, subject to the current download, license, and use conditions stated in the Mozilla Common Voice dataset card [18], that are ideal for visualizing waveforms, spectrograms, and features.Because the clips are short and easy to load, they let a newcomer see each stage of this chapter clearly before moving to the noisier broadcast and telephone data of later chapters. The companion notebook uses it for this purpose; report the release version and validated-hour count when you do.

Dataset Spotlight: SADA, the Saudi Audio DatasetSADA [19] is a large Saudi Arabic broadcast corpus with multiple dialects, speaker and gender labels, and defined splits, released under the license and access conditions specified in its dataset documentation.It is valuable because it adds spontaneous Gulf-dialect material to a landscape long dominated by MSA broadcast data, which makes it well suited to the dialect-balancing and per-dialect reporting practices above. When using it, report the version, the license, the per-dialect hours, the speaker metadata, and the official splits.

Dataset Spotlight: CasablancaCasablanca [15] is a multidialectal Arabic speech corpus spanning several dialects with transcriptions and annotations for dialect, gender, and code-switching, released under the license and access conditions in its documentation.Because it provides supervised dialectal data across many varieties, it is well suited to training and, especially, to honestly evaluating end-to-end dialect systems. Report the version, the license, the per-dialect hours, and the official splits when you use it.

Dataset Spotlight: AswatAswat [18] is a curated, manually cleaned corpus of about 732 hours of unlabeled Arabic speech (roughly two-thirds MSA) assembled for self-supervised pretraining.Because it is large and unlabeled, it is well suited to continual pretraining: continue the self-supervised objective on Aswat to move a multilingual encoder toward Arabic before fine-tuning on a small labeled set. Report the version and the hours used.

Dataset Spotlight: the Open Universal Arabic ASR LeaderboardThe Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard [44] benchmarks open Arabic recognizers across multiple multi-dialect test sets under one framework, reporting robustness, adaptation, and efficiency, not accuracy alone.It is useful precisely because it compares models on dialects rather than a single pooled set, which surfaces the per-dialect gaps that a headline number hides. Treat it as a reference point, and still report your own per-dialect results with the version and splits.

Dataset Spotlight: the NADI speech shared tasksThe NADI shared tasks are the field's shared yardstick for Arabic dialect processing. After several text editions at the country and province level, the speech subtasks arrived: dialect identification, dialectal recognition, and diacritic restoration, each with held-out test sets and a common scoring protocol. The editions keep coming and the leading scores keep moving, so treat the series as a protocol rather than as a result. Build against the splits of whichever edition is current, name that edition wherever a number is reported, and give per-dialect figures on those splits, which is the clearest way to show real progress.

Dataset Spotlight: Arabic synthesis corporaArabic TTS rests on a few carefully recorded corpora. SASSC is a standard MSA single-speaker corpus recorded by a professional speaker in studio conditions [32]; ClArTTS provides Classical Arabic suitable for recitation-style synthesis [23]; and ArVoice adds multi-speaker MSA material for more varied synthesis, useful for speaker diversity but not by itself a complete dialectal TTS resource [19]. Balanced-corpus design, choosing text that covers the sounds and contexts of the language efficiently, makes the most of limited recording time [33]. State the corpus, its speaker coverage, and its diacritization quality in any result.

Dataset Spotlight: Arabic translation and understanding resourcesThree resources anchor Arabic work here. CoVoST 2 provides Arabic-to-English speech-translation data and is the common starting point for end-to-end systems [3]. TEDxTN adds a three-way, code-switched Tunisian Arabic and English corpus, capturing the dialect and code-switching that real speech contains [4]. TARIC-SLU is a Tunisian spoken-language-understanding benchmark with intent and slot annotations [20]. State the corpus, its dialect coverage, and its train and test splits, and keep test speakers and dialogues disjoint from training.

Dataset Spotlight: L2AraSpeech, and the corpora that do not existL2AraSpeech is the corpus the pronunciation half of this chapter can point at: recordings from 220 non-native speakers of varied national and linguistic backgrounds reading 25 sentences and 61 minimal pairs chosen by linguists who teach Arabic to non-native speakers, with 60 of those speakers annotated for pronunciation errors, released through IEEE Dataport in raw, processed and annotated form under a licence for non-commercial research [12]. The minimal pairs are the part to look at first, because a minimal pair is the experiment this chapter keeps describing: two words that differ in exactly one sound, so a system that scores the pair correctly has scored the contrast rather than the word. The other two populations are still waiting. For disordered Arabic speech there is no substantial corpus at all, which is why the peer-reviewed Arabic work augments healthy speech instead of recording atypical speech, and why the personalization result this chapter relies on comes from English. For children there is a released Arabic set, Levantine classroom recordings that show how far a mainstream recognizer falls on child speech, still a preprint and still small. All three demand strict ethical and privacy governance, with guardian consent for children and speaker control for clinical data, and any report should state the population, the consent basis and the per-group results.

Dataset Spotlight: ArFake and VoxlectArFake is the first multi-dialect Arabic spoofed-speech dataset, cloned from the Casablanca corpus and released with detector baselines, and Voxlect is a cross-dialect benchmark over more than two million labelled utterances from thirty corpora, which is the kind of resource the fairness auditing in this chapter needs. Together they let Arabic security and fairness work move from anecdote to measurement. Two cautions travel with them. ArFake’s most convincing audio came from a single generator, which its own authors say may limit how far a detector trained on it generalizes, so treat a good score on it as a floor rather than a certificate. And Voxlect classifies dialects; it is not a licence to skip recording the speech your own system will actually meet. Report per dialect, and against the generators or the conditions a deployed system will really face.

Dataset Spotlight: Common Voice Arabic for a first projectThe crowd-sourced, openly licensed Common Voice Arabic corpus is the fastest way to a first end-to-end run, because anyone can download it and its CC0 public-domain dedication permits broad reuse [1].Its read speech and uneven dialect coverage make it a starting point rather than a final corpus, and any experiment using it should report the exact release version, since the dataset grows with every release.
